I have completed the investigation. The working tree remains untouched (verified clean; all scratch analysis lived in the OS temp directory, outside the repository). Below is the full audit.
---
# Sutra Full Audit
Method note: this environment had no browser/computer-use access, so UI/UX findings are derived from first-hand reading of the shell markup (Sutra.html), render code, stylesheets, e2e assertions, and documentation — not from clicking through the live product. Everything else is based on direct inspection of source, tests, schemas, and CI.
## Executive Summary
Sutra is two very different codebases wearing one repository. Around the edges it is some of the most disciplined frontend engineering I have audited in the "no-build static app" genre: an E2E-encrypted sync engine with a genuinely deterministic merge, a persistence core with compare-and-swap writes and mandatory readback verification, a fail-closed migration registry, a real sanitizer, adversarial backup-tampering tests, and a CI that ships exactly the bytes it tested. At the center sits src/core/app.js: **85,393 lines / 4.85 MB** of global-scope classic script containing ~4,000 functions, 253 distinct registered window globals, 374 innerHTML assignments, and ~318 empty catch blocks — with **zero executable unit coverage**, guarded by a static check that literally fails if the file shrinks below 80,000 lines / 4.5 MB (scripts/lib/core-runtime-integrity.mjs:5-6). That last fact is the thesis of this audit in miniature: the verification system and the project's own stated architecture goal are in open conflict, and the monolith is winning.
| Dimension | Score | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Engineering / Codebase | **6** | Bimodal: exemplary islands (sync, persistence, safety layer) inside a monolith with duplication families and dead defensive paths |
| Architecture | **5** | Documented, rational, self-aware — but center-of-mass concentration with extraction program stalled (1 file extracted into src/state/) |
| Reliability | **8** | CAS saves, readback verification, migration quarantine, cross-tab conflict surfacing, startup watchdog — best-in-class for this genre |
| Maintainability | **4.5** | 85k-line file, 15 divergent escapers, 8 date formatters, size-floor ratchet against decomposition, textual "contract tests" |
| UI | **6.5** | Token system + strong a11y signals + disciplined mobile layer, undermined by cascade debt, hex tail, mixed event regimes |
| UX | **6.5** | Thoughtful microcopy, consolidated onboarding, connected actions — vs. 14 top-level destinations straining the "calm default" promise |
| Performance | **6** | No virtualization, wholesale innerHTML rebuilds, 4.85 MB single-script parse; benchmarks exist but are advisory-only |
| Testing | **7** | Real breadth and occasional brilliance (fuzz-tested merge); dragged down by sleep-laden specs, tautological tail, Chromium-only PR gate |
| Security / Privacy Engineering | **7.5** | Strong crypto/sanitizer/RLS; 'unsafe-inline' script CSP + runtime CDN loads undercut the story |
| Overall Product Coherence | **6** | The daily loop is real in code, but the product carries visible sediment of "everything workspace" ambitions |
---
## What Is GOOD
Ranked strongest-first:
1. **The canonical save path is production-grade distributed-systems engineering.**
performCommitAppDataWithHealth (src/core/app.js:7195-7284) serializes an immutable detached snapshot, persists via workspaceDb.writeIf(...) conditioned on the canonical hash (CAS), throws WorkspaceConflictError instead of clobbering a newer cross-tab commit, advances its base only after the atomic commit boundary, then performs a mandatory readback hash verification raising PartialWriteError. Commits run through a serialized promise queue so failures don't stall later saves. Sync, Drive, and cloud auto-backup hooks are each individually wrapped so they can never block local saving. This is the correct design and it is correctly implemented.
2. **The sync engine (src/sync/, ~3,900 lines across 8 pure modules) is the intellectual high point of the codebase.**
Fully dependency-injected and Node-testable; deterministic merge keyed on (lamport, deviceId) tie-breaks; content-hashed conflict IDs stable across replays; conservative LCS-based three-way HTML block merge that returns "conflict" rather than guessing; delete-vs-edit preserves the edit; crash-atomic end-of-cycle commits in one IndexedDB transaction; snapshot cursors taken from AAD-authenticated envelope metadata (a hostile server cannot make a client skip ops); stable opIds with server-side dedupe; Lamport high-water persisted before any push. Crypto is correct where it counts: PBKDF2-SHA-256 at 600k iterations clamped on both wrap and unwrap, fresh 96-bit CSPRNG IVs per AES-GCM encryption, non-extractable keys, and four distinct AAD domains binding vault/wrap/op/snapshot/asset contexts (src/sync/sync-crypto.js). Preserve all of it.
3. **The core safety layer is coherent and genuinely fail-closed.**
dom-safety.js implements an allowlist sanitizer that drops dangerous subtrees wholesale, strips control-char URL obfuscation, rejects protocol-relative URLs, forces noopener noreferrer, allowlists inline-style properties with numeric bounds, and degrades to escaped text on any sanitizer exception. migrations.js validates before mutating, clones input, quarantines bad-shaped data instead of deleting it, passes future versions through untouched, and flags destructive steps. startup-health.js is false-alarm-resistant (watchdog + rechecks) and offers Reload / Safe Mode / emergency export while explicitly telling users not to clear site data — exactly right for local-first. error-reporter.js scrubs bearer tokens and API keys from diagnostics.
4. **Testing asserts outcomes, not vibes — where modules are pure.**
tests/unit/sync-merge.test.mjs includes a seeded randomized convergence property test over 25 seeds, direction-independent conflict IDs, lost-ack echo tolerance, and device-id privacy leak checks. tests/e2e/encrypted-backups.spec.mjs decodes exported envelopes and asserts sentinels (note titles, attachment bytes, API keys) do not leak, verifies KDF parameters, salt/IV uniqueness, and byte-flip tamper rejection without mutating local state. scripts/round-trip-check.mjs computes field sets from four independent sites and asserts parity against the persistence inventory — a genuine cross-artifact consistency engine. scripts/sutra-academic-engines-check.mjs executes grade math and asserts computed values. The guardrails are a fingerprint-ratchet with a self-test proving the scanner fires on hostile fixtures.
5. **CI tests the artifact it ships.**
.github/workflows/deploy.yml runs the browser matrix against .deploy/, uploads that same artifact to Pages, then live-smokes the deployment. Actions pinned to 40-char SHAs, enforced by a dedicated check. For a project whose AGENTS.md makes "the tested artifact is the deployed artifact" a principle, this is honored in machinery, not just prose.
6. **Service worker and offline posture is conservative and user-consenting.** Network-first navigations, cache admission only for 200 && type === 'basic', install aborts if critical assets are missing (partial runtime can never take control), skipWaiting only behind an explicit "Reload safely" banner, paired app-side stale-asset-skew detection that distinguishes cache skew from real save failure (app.js:7344-7427).
7. **Documentation discipline is unusual and mostly earned.** An AGENTS.md that actually matches what's in the tree, a load-order-conscious architecture doc, 43 feature docs, privacy/security docs, and honest legacy quarantine (styles/legacy/ extracted 1:1 at identical cascade positions).
8. **Individual feature modules show the team knows how to do it right when small:** mobile-nav.js (583 lines) builds DOM exclusively with createElement/textContent, implements dialog semantics, focus trap/restoration, Escape + browser-Back dismissal, scroll lock, reduced-motion honoring, and derives routes from canonical tab controls. homework.js documents a real fixed bug in comments and passes unknown studio payloads through untouched.
9. **Hygiene positives worth naming:** zero eval/new Function (with a comment explaining why a hand-written parser exists — CSP awareness baked in), effectively zero TODO/FIXME debt markers, only 4 stray console.logs in 534k lines, and an onboarding controller that openly documents consolidating four competing first-run flows into one canonical path.
---
## What Is MID
1. **The extraction program has stalled while the checks calcify around the monolith.**
src/state/ — whose charter is "pure defaults and normalizers extracted from app.js" — contains exactly one 66-line file, while real normalizers (normalizeWorkspacePreferences, getDefaultAppData, …) remain closure-bound. Meanwhile core-runtime-integrity.mjs enforces MIN_APP_BYTES = 4_500_000 / MIN_APP_LINES = 80_000. These floors were presumably anti-gutting tripwires, but they now make every sanctioned decomposition a failing build. ~21 "contract" unit tests read app.js as text and pass when strings appear. Severity: High over time. Needs redesign of both the extraction plan and the gates that measure progress.
2. **CSP undermines the security architecture it protects.**
Both Sutra.html:6 and vercel.json ship script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com https://unpkg.com .... 'unsafe-inline' exists partly because Sutra.html contains 264 inline onclick= handlers and several inline <script> blocks. Additionally, import features fetch third-party libraries at runtime from unpkg/cdnjs (mammoth, xlsx.full.min.js — seen at the loadExternalScript call site in app.js). That's a supply-chain surface (no SRI mentioned), an offline gap for docx/xlsx import, and a privacy expansion beyond "fresh startup makes no third-party requests" (startup itself is clean; these are user-triggered). Severity: Medium. Fix direction is mechanical: event delegation to kill inline handlers, vendor mammoth/xlsx like jszip/pdf.js already are, drop CDN from script-src.
3. **Duplication families are the largest correctness risk in the feature layer.**
15 local HTML-escapers (two inside app.js beside the canonical SutraDOMSafety.escapeHtml), 8 local YYYY-MM-DD date-key formatters (timezone-divergence waiting to happen), 3 dialog regimes, 3 timer regimes, and at least 3 competing deadline/priority scorers (app.js:20614 weighted score, student-engine.js:39 priorityScore, ap-study.js:956 entity score) despite an explicit "reuse canonical ranking engines" principle. Individually small; together they guarantee behavioral drift between surfaces that are supposed to agree. Severity: Medium-High cumulatively.
4. **Test quality is highly uneven.**
Best-in-class specs (encrypted backups, sync, mobile-nav) coexist with 99 waitForTimeout sleeps across 23 specs, near-tautological assertions ("app boots" ≡ document.body.children.length > 0 in chaos-persistence.spec.mjs:33-38), unasserted pageerror collectors, and per-spec reimplementations of completeOnboarding bootstrap helpers. PR CI runs Chromium-on-Ubuntu only; Firefox/WebKit/mobile run weekly. No type checking anywhere, no coverage measurement at all — nobody knows what fraction of app.js the corpus touches. Severity: Medium.
5. **Styling architecture is token-driven at the core, accreted everywhere else.**
tokens.css is a clean semantic contract, but styles.css is 35,315 lines holding half of all CSS with 14 separate :root blocks (36 repo-wide across 11 files), ~996 raw hex colors in its component zone, and dark mode implemented as ~221 per-selector patch blocks rather than token remapping. responsive/mobile.css loads at line 8290 of the shell with 25 sheets after it, which is precisely why it carries 587 !important flags. There is no prefers-color-scheme support anywhere — no auto dark mode. 53 ad-hoc breakpoints including off-by-one pairs (767/768/769, 1024/1025). Severity: Medium; incremental cleanup viable, eventual consolidation desirable.
6. **Backend ops-log grows forever.** supabase/sync-schema.sql has no pruning of acked ops — the engine's own comment assumes compaction enables server-side trimming (sync-engine.js:186-188), but nothing realizes it. Client-visible failure mode eventually (quota-exceeded pauses sync). Severity: Medium, latency-long.
7. **Repo hygiene.** Tracked clutter: commit-reorg.bat (one-off reorg debris at repo root), the unreferenced 366 KB noteflow-classic/noteflow.html, an orphan extension/ (7 files), and five loose root markdown files (info.md, TUTORIAL.md, SUTRA_GUIDE.md, design-qa.md) competing with the canonical docs/ tree. Untracked but disk-hostile: ~4.6 GB across launch-film/ (2 GB, 5,874 files), .tmp/ (2.5 GB, 80k files), pitch decks. Severity: Low-Medium; friction cost, not correctness.
8. **Accessibility foundations are strong but with soft spots:** 232 :focus-visible rules and 57 reduced-motion blocks are excellent signals, but only 9 uses of sr-only, 100 outline: none/0 sites needing pairing verification, sub-44px targets in places (36–38px timer/toolbar buttons in mobile.css:577-677 against the project's own --sutra-target-min: 2.75rem), and thin prefers-contrast coverage (2 blocks). Severity: Medium-Low.
---
## What Is BAD
1. **src/core/app.js as the application center of mass — systemic, High severity.**
85,393 lines; 225+ top-level functions (4,039 total function occurrences); 253 assigned window globals; 1,442 try blocks; 374 innerHTML sites; 318 empty catches within this file alone (457 repo-wide); section banners revealing numbered-section bookkeeping ("Section 17", "Section 25") characteristic of years of accretion. Consequences are concrete: no executable unit coverage is possible (the test infra even built a custom brace-scanner, tests/helpers/extract-function.mjs, purely to slice functions out of the string), regressions surface late through uneven e2e, review diffs are unreviewable at scale, and every new contributor must absorb a 4.85 MB context. This is not a style complaint — it is the mechanism by which every other risk in this audit persists.
2. **innerHTML-string building as the dominant rendering strategy — systemic, Medium-High severity.**
465 innerHTML assignment sites across src/, 207 inline style= attributes inside JS-built markup, and 15 divergent escapers guarding them. The canonical sanitizer and guardrail ratchet mitigate actual injection today, but the pattern means correctness depends on every one of hundreds of call sites choosing (and using!) the right local esc. One missed escape in a template literal loop (e.g., app.js:11395 college-hub tables, homework.js:2385) is a stored-XSS-in-local-workspace bug class the architecture otherwise works hard to prevent.
3. **Silent-loss edges in otherwise loud systems — localized, Medium severity each.**
- credential-vault.js:357-360: decrypt failure returns null — remembered secrets vanish without reportError.
- sync-merge.js:300-319: concurrent divergence of a >20-version page history silently trims oldest versions.
- Homework legacy-mirror write failures console-only (app.js:21187-21191).
- safe-storage.get() returns the raw string on JSON parse failure while sessionGet() returns the fallback — inconsistent contracts callers must defend against.
These violate the project's own "data loss must be visible" principle in narrow but real ways.
4. **Vestigial defensive code that lies — localized, Low severity but telling.**
flow-assistant.js references window.pages / window.tasks / window.timeBlocks 34 times as fallback data sources; I verified **nothing ever assigns those globals anywhere in src/**. Every such fallback reads undefined forever. Harmless today, actively misleading to maintainers, and symptomatic of the assistant module's 8,197-line size hiding dead paths from review.
5. **The verification system rewards bloat — architectural, High severity (cross-cutting #1).**
Restated deliberately as its own item: minimum-size floors, required-fragment lists, and indentation-sensitive regexes in round-trip-check.mjs mean the toolchain structurally punishes the exact refactor AGENTS.md mandates ("Continue decomposing risky portions of app.js only through small, tested seams"). A team that did the right thing would go red. This converts technical debt from accident into policy.
---
## Architecture Assessment
What Sutra actually has is a **hub-and-spoke global-scope architecture with an emerging port-and-adapter ring**: a monolithic hub (app.js) owning state, persistence, and most views; a safety ring loaded before everything (safe-storage, error-reporter, dom-safety, feature-guard, migrations, startup-health); pure domain/sync spokes (src/domain/, src/state/, src/sync/) that are dual-mode Node-testable modules communicating through injected dependencies; and a feature layer (src/features/) that consumes sanctioned seams (SutraHomeworkStore.subscribe, SutraModalManager, event bus topics) alongside a thick residue of ~20 directly-invoked hub functions (setActiveView ×25, persistAppData ×13).
What scaled well: the safety ring, pure sync/domain modules, the persistence coordinator, docs discipline, and the deploy-artifact pipeline. The seam pattern demonstrably works — homework, notifications, PDF workspace, and slides were all built against it.
What is straining: everything that stayed in the hub. Load order is load-bearing across 112+ script tags and 44 stylesheets scattered through three zones of an 8,915-line HTML file; folder structure is explicitly "an organizational map only." Global namespace collisions are managed by a baseline JSON inventory rather than prevented by construction. The architecture is not wrong for its constraints — the no-build choice is defensible and consistently executed — but it has passed the scale at which "one big file plus conventions" can be held in any single head, and the tooling now enforces staying past that point.
## Code Quality Assessment
Naming is generally good and vocabulary-consistent (canonical student terms throughout). Comments are unusually substantive — they explain why, document fixed bugs, and record invariants; comment density (~4,600 comment lines in app.js alone) is a genuine asset. The debt concentrates in four patterns: (1) copy-paste utility divergence (escapers/date-formatters/toast-shims); (2) empty-catch normalization (457 sites; many legitimate focus/close guards, but examples like school-schedule.js:1128 persisting mutated data then swallowing a render failure cross the line); (3) typeof-guard integration boilerplate repeated in every module instead of a single resolution helper; (4) dead/vestigial paths (undefined-global fallbacks, redundant transport branch at sync-transport.js:358-364). Abstraction quality is high in the pure modules and inconsistent in view code. Readability of the monolith is aided by banners but doomed by volume.
## Reliability / Data Integrity Assessment
This is Sutra's strongest pillar. Beyond the save path detailed above: hydration refuses to mark complete until confirmed; saves requested before hydration queue; import-time guards suppress stale editor state; cross-tab races resolve through CAS + publish/subscribe commit notifications; migrations quarantine rather than discard; export failures remain visible until a complete export succeeds; quota failures classify and surface through a durable banner with a working emergency-export button. Failure surfaces are layered and mostly non-overlapping (recovery alertdialog vs. save-failure banner vs. degraded badges vs. toasts). Remaining risks are the silent-loss edges listed in BAD §3, the narrow sync apply-window TOCTOU (engine isSaveIdle() check → applyMergedWorkspace depends on debounce-flush discipline), and the theoretical possibility that IndexedDB corruption scenarios outpace even verified writes (readback catches partial writes, not bit-rot on both ends of a verified round-trip).
## Testing Assessment
Quantity: 91 unit files (~520 tests, ~8,700 lines), 91 e2e specs (~19,600 lines), ~30 static gates in check:all, benchmarks. Quality: excellent-to-exemplary for pure modules; adequate-but-sleepy for flows; tautological in a tail. The decisive gap is structural: the highest-risk file in the repository contributes **zero** executable unit tests and is instead "tested" by string presence, while the gate enforcing its required fragments also enforces its minimum girth. Confidence verdict: high for sync/migrations/crypto/academic math; moderate for user flows (Chromium-only PR gate, sleeps, helper drift); low for app.js internals and cross-browser desktop behavior (single-OS CI despite a desktop-installed PWA).
## Performance Assessment
Likely bottlenecks, in order: (1) cold-start parse/execute of a 4.85 MB classic script plus 649 KB HTML with 77 view containers and 1,448 ids — cached well by the SW after first visit, heavy on first load and low-end devices; (2) wholesale innerHTML list rebuilds with no virtualization and zero IntersectionObserver usage (40 requestAnimationFrame and 16 MutationObserver uses suggest awareness, but large-workspace scaling rests on the advisory-only benchmark suite — which does at least exercise 1,000-note and 1,200-task seeds); (3) 89 debounce sites indicate hot-path churn being papered over per-feature rather than batched centrally; (4) CSS: 69k lines across 44 sheets with heavy !important resolution. Nothing here is fatal at student-scale data; everything compounds as workspaces grow.
## Security & Privacy Assessment
Strong where it matters most: encrypted backups assert absence-of-plaintext in tests; provider adapters receive ciphertext only; secrets are stripped across export paths and verified by automated checks; sync crypto is textbook-correct (parameters cited above); Supabase RLS denies direct table access outright with RPC-derived ownership, CAS vault keys under advisory locks, exact-path Storage policies; the local PIN lock honestly disclaims encryption-at-rest and verifies written config by readback; Assistant memory blocks sensitive categories. Deductions: 'unsafe-inline' + CDN script sources (fixable, see MID §2); runtime-fetched unpkg/cdnjs libraries without SRI; PIN lacks attempt-rate limiting (documented, acceptable); feature-guard's awaited-rejection caveat contradicting its header claim; credential-vault silent nulls.
## UI Audit
Strongest aspects (from code): a real token contract with a documented z-index ladder and 44px target variable; extensive ARIA in static markup (878 attributes, 229 roles, labeled inputs, polite live regions); a purpose-built responsive layer with safe-area handling, coarse-pointer hover suppression, and iOS zoom prevention; deliberate legacy style quarantine. Weakest aspects: visual consistency is maintained by convention across 69k lines of CSS rather than enforced by tokens — the ~1,000 hardcoded hex values and per-component dark patches mean themes will drift; three coexisting "redesign" generations are visible in the sheet names themselves (workspace-overrides.css, today-redesign.css, macos26-redesign.css, settings-redesign.css, homework-redesign.css) — the interface is archaeology you can read from the filenames; mixed interaction idioms (264 inline onclick alongside 774 addEventListener calls in app.js alone); loading-state vocabulary absent (0 skeleton indicators) while empty states exist (29 signals).
## UX Audit
The intended loop (capture → due → next step → notes → schedule → review → backed up) is visibly implemented in code: Daily Thread computes next-best-action from a unified deadline aggregator, contextualizes review debt and overload days, and attaches connected actions (Open/Schedule/Focus/Complete) with genuinely good microcopy ("one focused block now keeps you ahead"). Onboarding was consolidated from four competing flows into one versioned controller with migrated legacy flags — evidence of active UX-debt repayment. Tensions: fourteen top-level destinations (today, homework, notes, timeline, apstudy, review, cramhub, collegeapp, life, business, courses, alldue, assistantview, settings) strain the "calm default" promise even with pack gating (getActiveWorkspaceMode() threads through renderers); confirm-dialog degradation to toasts in shimmed modules (homework.js:84-85) can turn a destructive confirmation into a passive message; implementation leaks into UX in small ways (e.g., pull-to-refresh announcing "Refreshed" unconditionally). First-run experience appears thoughtfully designed; advanced-user depth (command palette, packs, Safe Mode) is present but discoverability of the boundary between daily and advanced surfaces is the open question I could not fully resolve without driving the UI.
## Mobile / Responsive Audit
Genuinely convincing as an adaptation strategy rather than a compression job: dedicated bottom nav deriving from canonical tabs (single route truth), Month→Day delegation on phones, horizontally contained Week view, safe-area math threaded through offsets, @supports guards, pointer-mode queries. Weaknesses are the cascade position tax (587 !importants), overflow-x: hidden as a mask rather than a fix, magic FAB stacking offsets (bottom: … +138px/196px/202px !important), and the breakpoint sprawl noted above. Automated responsive checks enforce targets and wrap-not-overflow behavior, which is more than most projects attempt.
## Consistency Audit
Recurring inconsistencies: storage channels (SutraSafeStorage vs. annotated direct-setItem fallbacks vs. bare reads in features); dialogs (three regimes); timers (three); ranking (three); escaping (fifteen); event binding (inline vs. addendum vs. delegation); theme patching (token remapping vs. selector patches); test bootstrap (shared-helper directory existing while every spec re-implements it). Architecturally consistent things worth crediting: error funnel usage, migration/versioning discipline, cache-stamping, and the seam-vs-monolith split is at least documented as hybrid rather than denied.
## Technical Debt Map
| Category | Items | Size estimate |
|---|---|---|
| **Structural** | app.js concentration + zero executable coverage + size-floor gates punishing extraction | Structural |
| **Significant** | innerHTML render strategy + escaper divergence; styling accretion (35k-line sheet, cascade position, hex tail); CSP/inline-handler regime | Significant |
| **Moderate** | duplication families (dates/dialogs/timers/ranking/toasts); uneven e2e quality + helper drift; no type checking/coverage measurement; Supabase op-log retention; silent-loss edges | Moderate |
| **Low** | repo clutter (tracked root strays, noteflow-classic, extension/, multi-GB untracked dirs); sr-only/outline/contrast gaps; minor nits (hhmmToMinutes range validation, lastSeen map growth, misfiled sutra-pro.css) | Low |
## Highest-Leverage Improvements
(Recommendations only — none implemented.)
1. **Make decomposition measurable and rewarded, then execute it.** Problem: 85k-line hub with zero executable coverage and gates that fail on shrinkage. Direction: replace size floors with behavior-preserving extraction milestones (each seam moves with its textual-contract test upgraded to an executable one); grow src/state/ and a views/ layer per the existing seam playbook (homework/slides prove the pattern works). Impact: unlocks maintainability, testability, and every other item below. Scope: **Architectural** (incremental, months).
2. **Harden the CSP story.** Remove inline handlers via delegation, vendor mammoth/xlsx locally (pdf.js/jszip precedent exists), drop cdnjs/unpkg from script-src, eliminate 'unsafe-inline' for scripts. Impact: closes the largest gap between privacy claims and enforcement; removes offline import gaps. Scope: **Medium**.
3. **Consolidate the utility families.** One escaper (already exists), one date-key formatter, one confirm/dialog resolver, one ranking engine entry point; enforce via the guardrail ratchet (add fingerprints for new local esc definitions). Impact: eliminates the divergence-bug class. Scope: **Medium**.
4. **Fix the mobile.css cascade position** (or introduce a deliberate final-layer override sheet) and retire hundreds of !importants. Impact: restores sane styling economics. Scope: **Small-Medium**, high care needed.
5. **Close silent-loss edges:** reportError on vault decrypt failure; revisit the 20-version merge cap; unify safe-storage.get parse-failure contract. Impact: honors the "data loss is visible" principle. Scope: **Small**.
6. **Raise the PR gate:** run the full browser matrix (or at least WebKit) per PR; add one macOS/Windows leg; deduplicate e2e bootstrap helpers; replace sleeps with polled expectations in the 23 flagged specs. Impact: catches the regression classes currently deferred to weekly cron. Scope: **Medium**.
7. **Server-side op-log pruning keyed to snapshot cursors.** Impact: prevents inevitable sync quota wall. Scope: **Small-Medium**.
8. **Auto dark mode via prefers-color-scheme** once tokens absorb the hex tail. Scope: **Medium** (depends on #4/token cleanup).
## Things I Would NOT Change
- **The no-build classic-script runtime model.** It is executed with unusual discipline (load-order docs, guardrails, cache stamps, artifact checks). A framework/bundler rewrite would destroy the compatibility guarantees that protect real user data for marginal gain.
- **Frozen identifiers and alias bridges** (noteflow_atelier_db, hwCourses:v2, legacy backup formats). They are load-bearing for user data, not unfinished renaming.
- **The sync engine's conservatism** (conflict-over-guess, AAD-everything, fail-closed cycles). Do not "simplify" the merge.
- **The CAS/readback save ceremony** — it looks paranoid and is exactly paranoid enough.
- **Migration quarantine philosophy** (preserve unknown fields, never downgrade future versions).
- **The verified-artifact CI pattern** and the guardrail-ratchet concept (its floors need changing; its ratchet mechanism is sound).
- **Startup-health's restraint** (never destructive, always dismissible, explicitly steers users away from clearing site data).
## Final Verdict
**How healthy is the codebase?** Healthier than its centerpiece suggests and less healthy than its docs imply. The periphery is robust, tested, documented, and actively hardened; the core is a monument that everyone involved clearly understands is temporary but which the tooling currently preserves in amber.
**Is the architecture still appropriate?** The model — yes. The proportions — no. Seams, safety layers, and pure modules are the right idea; they cover perhaps the outer 30% of the code while the inner 70% remains unextractable in practice.
**What will become painful as Sutra grows?** Any change touching multiple hub sections (unreviewable diffs), any new engineer onboarding (4.85 MB context), any performance work (no instrumentation culture), and eventually sync server costs (op-log growth).
**Does the product feel cohesive?** In intent, strongly — the daily loop, microcopy, and connected actions are real. In surface area, strained: fourteen destinations, three style generations, and duplicate subsystems are the visible sediment of ambition outrunning consolidation. The current AGENTS.md priorities (simplification, deduplication) are the correct diagnosis.
**Production-grade vs prototype-grade:** Production-grade: persistence, sync, crypto, backups/migrations, SW/offline, CI/artifact pipeline, docs. Prototype-grade in polish only, not correctness: view rendering layer, theming breadth, parts of the assistant module, the e2e tail.
**Largest risks:** (1) continued growth of app.js under gates that forbid shrinking it; (2) the innerHTML/escaper-divergence combination; (3) test-confidence asymmetry masking hub regressions until e2e.
**What would concern an inheriting engineer most?** Opening app.js and discovering the "temporary monolith" has a legal minimum size.
**What would impress them most?** That a solo-authored static app has fuzz-tested merge semantics, tamper-detecting backup tests, and a save path most funded teams never build — and that it admits its own weaknesses in writing.
---
**GOOD:** Sync engine and cryptography; canonical save path (CAS + readback + conflict surfacing); safety layer (sanitizer, migrations, startup health, error funnel); adversarial testing culture; verified-artifact CI; documentation honesty.
**MID:** CSP with 'unsafe-inline' + runtime CDN loads; styling accretion and mobile cascade tax; duplication families; uneven e2e quality and Chromium-only PR gating; stalled extraction program; missing op-log retention; repo clutter.
**BAD:** The 85k-line hub with zero executable coverage, guarded by minimum-size gates that punish the mandated fix; innerHTML-as-renderer with fifteen divergent escapers; scattered silent-loss edges.
**Biggest strength:** Data trustworthiness — Sura treats user data with a level of engineering paranoia that is rare anywhere and nearly unheard of in this genre.
**Biggest weakness:** The center cannot hold, and the tooling currently forbids moving it.
**Most important next investment:** A measured, gate-compatible extraction program for app.js — converting its textual contract tests into executable ones seam by seam — because every other improvement on this list becomes cheaper the moment the hub stops being indivisible.
